answer.rationale: With the line running at 94% of committed volume and no buffer, any supplier transition risk (onboarding, integration, invoicing setup) is amplified even if the low-cost vendor's quote alone satisfies the 18% mandate on paper. Memory_c4 indicates that benchmarking against market rates during renewal negotiations previously moved the incumbent on both price and terms without disrupting service continuity, and memory_c6 suggests longer-term commitments can lower unit cost without narrowing scope—both point toward negotiating with the incumbent using the low-cost quote as leverage, achieving cost reduction while avoiding the delivery risk inherent in a mid-cycle vendor switch with zero buffer. I verified memory_c4 (negotiation track record) and memory_c2 (switch track record) to confirm neither is an overly rosy retrospective before committing, since the switch option is tempting on cost alone but carries unverified downstream delivery risk given current capacity constraints. Renewal alone (c1) doesn't address the mandate; deferral (c5) isn't viable given the 14-day hard expiration; second-sourcing (c3) is valuable but doesn't resolve the primary contract expiration this cycle. This is a single-cycle capacity-limited decision, so I'm prioritizing the action that addresses both the cost mandate and the risk constraint simultaneously.
